title: Time value of money and choosing projects
subtitle: A rupee today is worth more than a rupee next year. Put every cash flow on one date and the choice becomes arithmetic.

why.title: Why money has a time value
why.body: Money can be invested to earn a return, so Rs 1,000 today can become more later. Simple interest is earned only on the principal; compound interest earns interest on interest: F = P(1 + i)ⁿ. At 10 % for 5 years, Rs 1,000 grows to Rs 1,611; equivalently Rs 1,000 in 5 years is worth only Rs 621 today.

eq.title: Equivalence and the cash-flow diagram
eq.body: Two cash flows are equivalent if they have the same worth at the same date and interest rate. A cash-flow diagram puts time on a horizontal axis, inflows as up arrows and outflows as down arrows. Below: invest 1,000 now and receive 350 at the end of each of 4 years, at MARR = 8 %.

factors.title: The six interest factors
factors.body:
To findGivenFactor
FP(1 + i)ⁿ
PF(1 + i)⁻ⁿ
PA[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1] / [i(1 + i)ⁿ]
APi(1 + i)ⁿ / [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]
FA[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1] / i
AFi / [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]

Annuity A is a uniform end-of-period payment. The present worth of 350 a year for 4 years at 8 % is 1159.24; repaying a Rs 1,000 loan over 4 years costs 301.92 a year.
factors.steps: P/A factor at 8 %, n = 4. Multiply by the annuity amount 350.

nom.title: Nominal and effective rates
nom.body: A nominal 12 % compounded monthly is 1 % per month; the effective annual rate is (1 + r/m)ᵐ − 1 = 12.68 %, more than 12 % because of within-year compounding. Always match the interest period to the payment period.
nom.steps: Nominal 18 % compounded quarterly: 4.5 % per quarter. Effective annual rate.

pw.title: Present worth and MARR
pw.body: The minimum attractive rate of return (MARR) is the least return the firm will accept. Project net present worth NPW = Σ Cₜ/(1 + MARR)ᵗ. If NPW > 0 the project earns more than MARR — accept. Project A at 8 %: NPW = −1000 + 350·(P/A) = 159.24; project B (invest 1,500, receive 500 a year) gives 156.06. Both are worth doing on their own; but only one can be built.

irr.title: Internal rate of return
irr.body: The IRR is the rate that makes NPW = 0. Accept if IRR > MARR. Project A: IRR ≈ 14.96 %; project B: 12.59 %. Both beat 8 %. The IRR is found by trial (or by the card’s solver) — there is no closed form for n > 4.
irr.steps: Try i = 15 %: NPW = −1000 + 350 × 2.855. That is almost zero, so the IRR is just under 15 %.

inc.title: Comparing alternatives: incremental analysis
inc.body: Only one of A, B can be built. The larger IRR does not always win, and a bigger investment is justified only if its extra money earns enough. Analyse the increment B − A: extra investment 500, extra return 150 a year, incremental IRR ≈ 7.71 %. That is below the MARR of 8 %, so the extra 500 is not worth spending: choose A. (Consistent with NPW(A) = 159.24 > NPW(B) = 156.06, even though B has the larger returns.) Compare equal-life options by NPW; unequal lives by annual worth, which repeats each as if replaced.
inc.steps: Incremental cash flow B − A. Incremental IRR vs MARR 8 %.

bc.title: Benefit–cost ratio and payback
bc.body: Public projects use B/C = PW(benefits)/PW(costs); accept if > 1. Payback is the time to recover the investment: simple payback for A = 1000/350 = 2.86 years. It ignores the time value and cash flows after payback, so use it only as a rough liquidity check.
